newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila expected to install new Zaire government.
newsitem.headline: Kabila expected to install new Zaire government.

text.p: Victorious guerrilla leaders vowed on Monday to change the political face of Zaire and self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila was expected in the capital Kinshasa to install a new administration.

Under pressure to form a broad-based government, the leadership of the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo said their priority was political re-education from peasant collectives upwards before national elections could be held.
The euphoria over the weekend rebel overthrow of the 32-year dictatorship of Mobutu Sese Seko was mixed with continuing violence in the capital of five million people.

The local Red Cross said it retrieved 22 bodies across the city on Monday, taking the death toll since the rebel takeover to 222. The dead were a mix of diehard Mobutu soldiers killed by Kabila's forces and irate civilians or looters shot by rebels.
Kabila's planning and development expert Babi Mbai was bombarded with questions about security when he sought to reassure the business community at a meeting in Kinshasa on Monday.
"It is planned that within a short period we will have 10,000 to 20,000 troops in Kinshasa to solve the problem of security," Mbai told his audience, mostly local businessmen.

With the rebels still mopping up pockets of resistance, Kabila was expected to arrive in Kinshasa on Tuesday from his temporary base in the southern city of Lubumbashi, according to official announcements by the United States and South Africa.

"We understand, based on meetings this morning, that Mr. Laurent Kabila plans to arrive in Kinshasa tomorrow, that he plans to formally establish an interim government by tomorrow evening," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
South Africa's President Nelson Mandela, who led last-ditch mediation in the Zaire conflict, made a similar announcement in Zimbabwe where he is on a state visit.
His deputy, Thabo Mbeki, said in Johannesburg that Kabila would announce a new government on Tuesday night. Mbeki met Kabila in Lubumbashi on Sunday.
In a statement redolent with the rhetoric of 1960s anti-colonialism, Kabila's Number Two urged patience over an election date.
"We must reawaken the population politically. It is our first duty," Kabila aide Deogratias Bugera told a news conference in Kinshasa on Monday.
"The aim is to avoid the possibility in the future that any one man can confiscate power," he said, accusing Mobutu of plundering what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations.
Despite Kabila's Marxist beginnings, there was no evident intention of establishing a communist-style state, as Bugera preached a need for economic independence and free enterprise.
Mobutu rested in Togo's capital Lome after leaving his jungle palace in his ancestral home region of Gbadolite on Zaire's northern border, a security source in Togo said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said the United Nations was ready to work with a new government but he added:
"We should not forget that apart from the alliance there have been other political opposition movements in Zaire and the other political movements will have to be brought in."

World powers voiced cautious support for Kabila, generally linking this to progress towards democratic rule. They included Germany, Japan and Italy following similar pledges by the United States, France, Italy and former colonial ruler Belgium.
South Africa, Libya and Kabila's key regional allies Rwanda and Burundi announced outright recognition.
The sprawling capital regained some of its bustle on Monday, the first working day after the dramatic overthrow of Mobutu.

In a strong sign of confidence in Kabila, the Zaire currency more than doubled in value against the dollar. Money changers on Kinshasa's "Wall Street" posted the zaire at about 70,000 to the U.S. currency against 185,000 to the dollar last week.
Traders said this had more to do with a desire to conform to rebel wishes than any sudden change in economic conditions.

Many city shops were open and traffic and people were out on the streets. Students chanted anti-Mobutu slogans in scattered demonstrations of support for Kabila and his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL).
The ferry crossing between Kinshasa and Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo across the river, remained blocked.
Newspapers appearing for the first time since Friday's climax to a seven-month rebel offensive toasted Kabila.
